title: Columnstore Indexes
description: Use columnar storage, segment elimination, and batch-mode execution to make analytical queries dramatically faster.

data.text: A rowstore index stores all columns of a row together, which is ideal when a query needs most columns for a few rows. A columnstore index stores each column separately and compresses it, which is ideal when a query scans millions of rows but touches only a few columns. SQL Server 2012 introduced nonclustered columnstore indexes; since SQL Server 2014 you can create a clustered columnstore index (CCI) directly on a table and make it the primary storage.

A clustered columnstore index replaces the table's heap or clustered index. Load data with bulk insert or `INSERT ... SELECT` in batches of at least 102,400 rows so each batch lands directly in a compressed rowgroup instead of the delta store.

data.title: Create a clustered columnstore index
data.content: Any existing clustered index must be dropped first; the CCI becomes the table's physical storage.

data.title: Watch the delta store
data.text: Small inserts and updates go into a rowstore delta store, which is queried alongside the compressed rowgroups. A delta store with millions of rows defeats the purpose of columnstore. Check `sys.dm_db_column_store_row_group_physical_stats` and rebuild the index to move rows into compressed rowgroups.

SQL Server 2016 made nonclustered columnstore indexes updatable, so an OLTP table can keep its B-tree clustered index and add a columnstore index for reporting. The optimizer can use that index to answer an analytical query without changing the write path.

data.title: Add a nonclustered columnstore index to an OLTP table
data.content: The index covers the columns the reporting query needs, so the query can scan compressed columns without touching the rowstore.
data.code:
CREATE NONCLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX NCCI_Orders_Analytics
ON dbo.Orders (OrderDate, CustomerId, ProductId, Quantity, Amount);
GO

SELECT
    DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1) AS Month,
    SUM(Amount) AS Revenue
FROM dbo.Orders
GROUP BY DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(OrderDate), MONTH(OrderDate), 1)
ORDER BY Month;

data.title: Order rows by date to improve segment elimination
data.content: The ORDER clause makes each compressed rowgroup cover a narrower date range, so a query for one month can skip most rowgroups.
data.code:
CREATE CLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX CCI_FactSales_Ordered
ON dbo.FactSales
ORDER (OrderDate, ProductId)
WITH (DROP_EXISTING = ON);

data.title: Interview angle: why not columnstore everything?
data.text: Columnstore is poor for single-row lookups and frequent updates, and it has data-type restrictions and higher build cost. It shines when queries scan a large fraction of a big table and aggregate a few columns. A common production design is a B-tree clustered index for the OLTP path plus a nonclustered columnstore index for reporting, or a partitioned table where recent partitions are rowstore and older partitions are columnstore.

data.title: Columnstore Indexes Key Points
points: Columnstore stores and compresses each column separately, which is ideal for large analytical scans.
Clustered columnstore indexes replace the table's rowstore storage; nonclustered columnstore indexes can coexist with a B-tree.
Batch-mode execution and segment elimination are the main performance wins.
Bulk load at least 102,400 rows per batch to avoid filling the delta store.
Updates and small inserts land in the delta store and need the tuple mover or an index rebuild.
Use columnstore for analytics, not for point lookups or heavy single-row OLTP.
